items.readable_text:
Content:
To solve logarithmic equations containing the natural logarithm [MATH: (\ln),] we can use the same method as usual: first isolate the logarithm, and then exponentiate both sides of the equation using the same base as the logarithm.

Content:
The key is to remember that the base of the natural logarithm is [MATH: e.]

Content:
To demonstrate, let's solve for [MATH: x] in the equation [MATH: \ln x = 2.]

Content:
To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is [MATH: e.] So, we use a base of [MATH: e] for the exponentiation as well:

Content:
[MATH: \ln x|= 2; e^{\ln x}|= e^{2}]

Content:
Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that [MATH: e^{\ln x} = x.]

Content:
Therefore, we get

Content:
[MATH: x|= e^{2}.]

Content:
So, the solution is [MATH: x=e^2.]

items.title: Solving Natural Logarithmic Equations

sections.normalized_html:
To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is [MATH: e.] So, we use a base of [MATH: e] for the exponentiation as well:

[MATH: \ln (4x + 5)|= 3; e^{\ln (4x + 5)}|= e^{3}]

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that [MATH: e^{\ln(4x+5)} = 4x+5.]

Therefore, we get

[MATH: 4x + 5|= e^{3}; 4x|= e^{3} − 5; x|= (e^{3} − 5)/(4).]

sections.normalized_html: Find the values of [MATH: x] such that [MATH: \ln(1-2x) + 5\ln(1-2x) = 4.]
sections.readable_text: Find the values of [MATH: x] such that [MATH: \ln(1-2x) + 5\ln(1-2x) = 4.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we rearrange our equation by collecting the like logarithmic terms, as follows:

[MATH: \ln (1 − 2x) + 5\ln (1 − 2x)|= 4; (1 + 5)\ln (1 − 2x)|= 4; 6\ln (1 − 2x)|= 4; \ln (1 − 2x)|= (2)/(3)]

To remove the natural logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the natural logarithm is [MATH: e,] so we use a base of [MATH: e] for the exponentiation as well:

[MATH: \ln (1 − 2x)|= (2)/(3); e^{\ln (1 − 2x)}|= e^{2/3}]

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that [MATH: e^{\ln(1-2x)} = 1-2x.]

Therefore, we get

[MATH: 1 − 2x|= e^{2/3}; 1 − 2x|= root(e^{2}, 3); − 2x|= root(e^{2}, 3) − 1; x|= − (root(e^{2}, 3) − 1)/(2); x|= (− root(e^{2}, 3) + 1)/(2); x|= (1 − root(e^{2}, 3))/(2).]
